claim: The incidence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has been increasing worldwide.
source: The incidence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has been increasing worldwide.
evidence: This is a general statement about MASLD prevalence trends, supported by established scientific literature.

claim: Gut-derived bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS) can travel via the portal vein to the liver and play an important role in producing hepatic pathology.
source: Since gut-derived bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS) can travel via the portal vein to the liver and play an important role in producing hepatic pathology
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract, supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Acyloxyacyl hydrolase (AOAH) is the eukaryotic lipase that inactivates LPS and oxidized phospholipids.
source: Acyloxyacyl hydrolase (AOAH), the eukaryotic lipase that inactivates LPS and oxidized phospholipids, is produced in the intestine, liver, and other organs.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about AOAH function, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: AOAH is produced in the intestine, liver, and other organs.
source: Acyloxyacyl hydrolase (AOAH), the eukaryotic lipase that inactivates LPS and oxidized phospholipids, is produced in the intestine, liver, and other organs.
evidence: This statement describes the tissue distribution of AOAH, supported by established knowledge.

claim: Aoah-/- mice accumulated more hepatic lipid than did Aoah+/+ mice when fed either normal chow or a high-fat diet for 28 weeks.
source: We fed mice either normal chow or a high-fat diet for 28 weeks and found that Aoah-/- mice accumulated more hepatic lipid than did Aoah+/+ mice.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the study comparing the two mouse strains.

claim: In young mice, before increased hepatic fat accumulation was observed, Aoah-/- mouse livers increased their abundance of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1.
source: In young mice, before increased hepatic fat accumulation was observed, Aoah-/- mouse livers increased their abundance of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1, and the expression of its target genes that promote fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements in young mice before disease development.

claim: Aoah-/- mouse livers increased expression of target genes that promote fatty acid synthesis.
source: In young mice, before increased hepatic fat accumulation was observed, Aoah-/- mouse livers increased their abundance of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1, and the expression of its target genes that promote fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data from the study.

claim: Aoah-/- mice increased hepatic expression of Cd36 and Fabp3, which mediate fatty acid uptake.
source: Aoah-/- mice also increased hepatic expression of Cd36 and Fabp3, which mediate fatty acid uptake
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements and established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claim: Aoah-/- mice decreased expression of fatty acid-oxidation-related genes Acot2 and Ppara.
source: and decreased expression of fatty acid-oxidation-related genes Acot2 and Ppara.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claim: Increasing AOAH abundance in the gut, bloodstream, and/or liver may be an effective strategy for preventing or treating MASLD.
source: Our results provide evidence that increasing AOAH abundance in the gut, bloodstream, and/or liver may be an effective strategy for preventing or treating MASLD.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The global prevalence of MASLD is currently about 25%.
source: Its global prevalence, currently about 25%, has been increasing (Diehl and Day, 2017; Fan et al., 2017; Younossi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MASLD may progress from nonalcoholic fatty liver to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, cirrhosis, and even hepatic cancer.
source: MASLD may progress from nonalcoholic fatty liver to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, cirrhosis, and even hepatic cancer (Friedman et al., 2018; Sheka et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gut-derived LPS may translocate into the portal venous system and traffic to the liver, triggering or exacerbating hepatic inflammation.
source: Gut-derived LPS may translocate into the portal venous system and traffic to the liver, triggering or exacerbating hepatic inflammation (Albillos et al., 2020; Carpino et al., 2020; Han et al., 2021; Kazankov et al., 2019; Leung et al., 2016; Munford, 1978; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: LPS molecules that contribute to MASLD pathogenesis are able to stimulate host cells because their lipid A structure is recognized by MD-2/TLR4 receptors.
source: The LPS molecules that contribute to MASLD pathogenesis are able to stimulate host cells because their lipid A structure is recognized by MD-2/TLR4 receptors (Ye et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and established knowledge about LPS recognition.

claim: Most γ-Proteobacteria such as Escherichia coli produce stimulatory hexaacyl LPS (with six acyl chains).
source: Most γ-Proteobacteria such as Escherichia coli produce stimulatory hexaacyl LPS (with six acyl chains) while Bacteroidetes produce non-stimulatory LPS that has four or five acyl chains (Anhê et al., 2021; d'Hennezel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bacteroidetes produce non-stimulatory LPS that has four or five acyl chains.
source: Most γ-Proteobacteria such as Escherichia coli produce stimulatory hexaacyl LPS (with six acyl chains) while Bacteroidetes produce non-stimulatory LPS that has four or five acyl chains (Anhê et al., 2021; d'Hennezel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MASLD is often associated with intestinal dysbiosis produced by increased abundance of γ-Proteobacteria.
source: MASLD is often associated with intestinal dysbiosis produced by increased abundance of γ-Proteobacteria, which leads to tissue inflammation and increased intestinal permeability that allows even more gut-derived LPS to reach the liver (Albillos et al., 2020; Aron-Wisnewsky et al., 2020a; Aron-Wisnewsky et al., 2020b; Mouries et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Increased abundance of γ-Proteobacteria leads to tissue inflammation and increased intestinal permeability that allows even more gut-derived LPS to reach the liver.
source: MASLD is often associated with intestinal dysbiosis produced by increased abundance of γ-Proteobacteria, which leads to tissue inflammation and increased intestinal permeability that allows even more gut-derived LPS to reach the liver (Albillos et al., 2020; Aron-Wisnewsky et al., 2020a; Aron-Wisnewsky et al., 2020b; Mouries et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Gut-derived LPS is known to induce hepatic inflammation and exacerbate MASLD.
source: Although gut-derived LPS is known to induce hepatic inflammation and exacerbate MASLD, how LPS influences hepatocyte fatty acid metabolism before MASLD develops has not been well understood.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: How LPS influences hepatocyte fatty acid metabolism before MASLD develops has not been well understood.
source: Although gut-derived LPS is known to induce hepatic inflammation and exacerbate MASLD, how LPS influences hepatocyte fatty acid metabolism before MASLD develops has not been well understood.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: AOAH is a highly conserved animal lipase.
source: Acyloxyacyl hydrolase (AOAH) is a highly conserved animal lipase that is mainly expressed in macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, microglia, dendritic cells, NK cells, and ILC1 cells (Munford et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: AOAH is mainly expressed in macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, microglia, dendritic cells, NK cells, and ILC1 cells.
source: Acyloxyacyl hydrolase (AOAH) is a highly conserved animal lipase that is mainly expressed in macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, microglia, dendritic cells, NK cells, and ILC1 cells (Munford et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: AOAH can inactivate Gram-negative bacterial LPSs by releasing two of the six fatty acyl chains present in the lipid A moiety.
source: It can inactivate Gram-negative bacterial LPSs by releasing two of the six fatty acyl chains present in the lipid A moiety (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which shows the mechanism of action.

claim: AOAH can deacylate/inactivate oxidized phospholipids and lysophospholipids, molecules that are known to contribute to MASLD.
source: It also can deacylate/inactivate oxidized phospholipids and lysophospholipids, molecules that are also known to contribute to MASLD (Sun et al., 2020; Zou et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AOAH is expressed by gut macrophages and dendritic cells and can inactivate bioactive LPS in feces.
source: We previously reported that AOAH is expressed by gut macrophages and dendritic cells and can inactivate bioactive LPS in feces (Cheng et al., 2023; Janelsins et al., 2014; Qian et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications.

claim: AOAH inactivates LPS in the liver, diminishing and shortening hepatic inflammation induced by bloodborne LPS.
source: AOAH also inactivates LPS in the liver, diminishing and shortening hepatic inflammation induced by bloodborne LPS (Ojogun et al., 2009; Shao et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Intestine-derived LPS can bind high-density lipoprotein 3 (HDL3) and be inactivated by AOAH as it traffics from the jejunum to the liver via the portal vein.
source: Han et al. found that intestine-derived LPS can bind high-density lipoprotein 3 (HDL3) and be inactivated by AOAH as it traffics from the jejunum to the liver via the portal vein (Han et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Aoah-/- mice fed either NC or HFD gained more weight than did Aoah+/+ control mice.
source: Aoah-/- mice fed either NC or HFD gained more weight than did Aoah+/+ control mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When fed either NC or HFD, the livers of Aoah-/- mice were heavier than those of Aoah+/+ control mice.
source: When they were fed either NC or HFD, the livers of Aoah-/- mice were heavier than those of Aoah+/+ control mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Aoah-/- mouse livers accumulated more lipid droplets than did the livers of Aoah+/+ mice.
source: Histological examination and Oil Red O staining revealed that Aoah-/- mouse livers accumulated more lipid droplets than did the livers of Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Aoah-/- mice developed more severe MASLD than did Aoah+/+ mice whether the mice were fed NC or HFD.
source: When we scored MASLD severity based on steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning degeneration, and inflammation, Aoah-/- mice developed more severe MASLD than did Aoah+/+ mice whether the mice were fed NC or HFD (Sheka et al., 2020; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by MASLD scoring data shown in Figure 1E and citation to the scoring method.

claim: When the mice were fed either NC or HFD, Aoah-/- mouse livers contained more triacylglycerol (TAG) than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers.
source: When the mice were fed either NC or HFD, Aoah-/- mouse livers contained more triacylglycerol (TAG) than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers, while livers from both mouse strains contained a similar amount of total cholesterol (TCHO, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Livers from both Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mouse strains contained a similar amount of total cholesterol.
source: When the mice were fed either NC or HFD, Aoah-/- mouse livers contained more triacylglycerol (TAG) than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers, while livers from both mouse strains contained a similar amount of total cholesterol (TCHO, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: When the mice were fed the HFD, Aoah-/- mice had higher serum levels of TAG, TCHO, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and free fatty acids than did Aoah+/+ mice.
source: When the mice were fed the HFD, Aoah-/- mice had higher serum levels of TAG, TCHO, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and free fatty acids than did Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by serum measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Aoah-/- mice fed HFD had significantly higher serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels than did control Aoah+/+ mice.
source: Aoah-/- mice fed HFD had significantly higher serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels than did control Aoah+/+ mice, suggesting that Aoah-/- mice experienced more severe liver inflammation and tissue damage (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by serum enzyme measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Aoah-/- mice experienced more severe liver inflammation and tissue damage when fed HFD.
source: Aoah-/- mice fed HFD had significantly higher serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels than did control Aoah+/+ mice, suggesting that Aoah-/- mice experienced more severe liver inflammation and tissue damage (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on elevated ALT and AST levels, which are markers of liver damage.

claim: When mice were fed the HFD, Aoah-/- mouse livers produced more pro-inflammatory Il6, Ifng, and anti-inflammatory Il10 mRNA than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers.
source: When mice were fed the HFD, Aoah-/- mouse livers produced more pro-inflammatory Il6, Ifng, and anti-inflammatory Il10 mRNA than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers, suggesting greater inflammation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Aoah-/- livers had more Timp1 (a pro-fibrosis gene) mRNA and less Mmp2 (an anti-fibrosis gene) mRNA than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers.
source: We also found that Aoah-/- livers had more Timp1 (a pro-fibrosis gene) mRNA and less Mmp2 (an anti-fibrosis gene) mRNA than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers (Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021), indicating that Aoah-/- mouse livers may be developing more severe fibrosis, although we did not detect fibrosis with Masson staining (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 2C and citation to literature about fibrosis genes.

claim: Aoah-/- mouse livers may be developing more severe fibrosis.
source: We also found that Aoah-/- livers had more Timp1 (a pro-fibrosis gene) mRNA and less Mmp2 (an anti-fibrosis gene) mRNA than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers (Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021), indicating that Aoah-/- mouse livers may be developing more severe fibrosis, although we did not detect fibrosis with Masson staining (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns, though histological fibrosis was not detected.

claim: When the mice were fed the HFD, Aoah-/- mouse livers contained more neutrophils, monocytes, and lipid-associated macrophages (hepatic LAMs) than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers.
source: We analyzed the myeloid cells in the liver (Daemen et al., 2021) and found that when the mice were fed the HFD, Aoah-/- mouse livers contained more neutrophils, monocytes, and lipid-associated macrophages (hepatic LAMs) (Remmerie et al., 2020; Su, 2002) than did Aoah+/+ mouse livers (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2D and E, with citations to methods and cell type definitions.

claim: When the mice were fed an HFD, the livers of Aoah-/- mice developed significantly greater inflammatory responses and tissue damage.
source: Collectively, when the mice were fed an HFD, the livers of Aoah-/- mice developed significantly greater inflammatory responses and tissue damage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental measurements presented in the study.

claim: AOAH was mainly expressed in Kupffer cells in the liver.
source: We found previously that AOAH was mainly expressed in Kupffer cells in the liver (Shao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: AOAH is expressed in Kupffer cells, monocytes, monocyte-derived cells, NK (circulating NK), and ILC1 (tissue resident NK) cells in mouse livers.
source: To confirm the previous results, we first consulted the single-cell RNA-seq analysis reported by Remmerie et al., 2020, who found that AOAH is expressed in Kupffer cells, monocytes, monocyte-derived cells, NK (circulating NK), and ILC1 (tissue resident NK) cells in mouse livers (Remmerie et al., 2020; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data from a cited study, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AOAH mRNA was present in Kupffer cells, monocytes, and NK cells but not in hepatocytes.
source: Using qPCR analysis, we found that AOAH mRNA was present in Kupffer cells, monocytes, and NK cells but not in hepatocytes, in keeping with previous findings (Shao et al., 2007; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and citation to previous findings.

claim: Aoah+/+ mouse livers but not Aoah-/- mouse livers had AOAH protein.
source: Western blot analysisanalysis confirmed that Aoah+/+ mouse livers but not Aoah-/- mouse livers had AOAH protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When Aoah+/+ mice aged or had an HFD, their hepatic AOAH expression increased.
source: When Aoah+/+ mice aged or had an HFD, their hepatic AOAH expression increased (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: AOAH was expressed in macrophages, monocytes, resident and circulating NK cells, and some T cells in human liver.
source: We also studied the expression of AOAH in human liver cells by analyzing the single-cell RNA-seq data obtained by Ramachandran et al., 2019; AOAH was expressed in macrophages, monocytes, resident and circulating NK cells, and some T cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data from a cited study, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: AOAH expression increased in liver macrophages and monocytes in MASLD patients.
source: AOAH expression increased in liver macrophages and monocytes in MASLD patients (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Aoah-/- mouse feces, liver, and plasma had higher bioactive LPS levels when Aoah-/- and Aoah+/+ mice were fed either NC or HFD.
source: We found that Aoah-/- mouse feces, liver, and plasma had higher bioactive LPS levels when Aoah-/- and Aoah+/+ mice were fed either NC or HFD (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by LPS activity measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: HFD increased gut permeability.
source: HFD increased gut permeability, but there was no permeability difference between Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice that were fed either NC or HFD for 28 weeks, suggesting that the increased hepatic LPS levels in Aoah-/- mouse livers were mainly caused by failure to inactivate LPS (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by gut permeability measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There was no permeability difference between Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice that were fed either NC or HFD for 28 weeks.
source: HFD increased gut permeability, but there was no permeability difference between Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice that were fed either NC or HFD for 28 weeks, suggesting that the increased hepatic LPS levels in Aoah-/- mouse livers were mainly caused by failure to inactivate LPS (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by gut permeability measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The increased hepatic LPS levels in Aoah-/- mouse livers were mainly caused by failure to inactivate LPS.
source: HFD increased gut permeability, but there was no permeability difference between Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice that were fed either NC or HFD for 28 weeks, suggesting that the increased hepatic LPS levels in Aoah-/- mouse livers were mainly caused by failure to inactivate LPS (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gut permeability was similar between genotypes.

claim: After the mice were fed HFD for 28 weeks, Aoah-/- mouse livers increased fatty acid uptake gene Fabp3 mRNA and fatty acid synthesis gene Fasn mRNA.
source: After the mice were fed HFD for 28 weeks, Aoah-/- mouse livers increased fatty acid uptake gene Fabp3 mRNA and fatty acid synthesis gene Fasn mRNA, changes that may have contributed to lipid accumulation (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 3H.

claim: AOAH may prevent hepatic lipid accumulation by diminishing bioactive LPS in the liver.
source: Thus, AOAH may prevent hepatic lipid accumulation by diminishing bioactive LPS in the liver.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing reduced LPS levels with AOAH.

claim: The expression of several fatty acid biosynthesis genes, such as Acacb, Acss2, Pcx, Acly, Fasn, and Scd1, was significantly increased in Aoah-/- mouse livers.
source: The expression of several fatty acid biosynthesis genes, such as Acacb (acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylase beta), Acss2 (acetyl-CoA synthetase 2), Pcx (pyruvate carboxylase), Acly (ATP citrate lyase), Fasn (fatty acid synthase), and Scd1 (stearoyl-coenzyme A desaturase 1), was significantly increased in Aoah-/- mouse livers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The fatty acid biosynthesis pathway was enriched in Aoah-/- mouse livers.
source: When we used gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) to analyze deferentially expressed genes, we found that the fatty acid biosynthesis pathway was enriched (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: mRNAs for enzymes involved in fatty acid oxidation (Acot2 and Ppara) decreased in Aoah-/- mouse livers.
source: In addition, mRNAs for enzymes involved in fatty acid oxidation (Acot2 [acyl-CoA thioesterase 2] and Ppara [peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α]) (Bougarne et al., 2018; Moffat et al., 2014) decreased (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 4D and citations to literature about these genes.

claim: Cd36 mRNA levels increased in Aoah-/- mouse livers.
source: while Cd36 (fatty acid uptake; Chen et al., 2022) mRNA levels increased in Aoah-/- mouse livers (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 4E and citation to literature about Cd36 function.

claim: FASN and SCD1 protein levels increased in Aoah-/- mouse livers.
source: We confirmed that FASN and SCD1 protein levels also increased in Aoah-/- mouse livers (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The livers of Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice had similar levels of Acsl1, Dgat2, and Pnpla2 mRNA.
source: yet the livers of Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice had similar levels of Acsl1, Dgat2, and Pnpla2 mRNA, suggesting that AOAH does not regulate hepatic TAG metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AOAH does not regulate hepatic TAG metabolism.
source: yet the livers of Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice had similar levels of Acsl1, Dgat2, and Pnpla2 mRNA, suggesting that AOAH does not regulate hepatic TAG metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TAG metabolism genes were not differentially expressed.

claim: AOAH reduces liver fat accumulation by diminishing the expression of fatty acid synthesis and uptake genes and increasing that of fatty acid oxidation genes.
source: These results suggest that AOAH reduces liver fat accumulation by diminishing the expression of fatty acid synthesis and uptake genes and increasing that of fatty acid oxidation genes.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the gene expression data presented in the study.

claim: Acaca, Fasn, and Scd1 are all target genes for sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1).
source: As Acaca, Fasn, and Scd1 are all target genes for sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1, encoded by Srebf1 gene), a key transcription factor for fatty acid biosynthesis, we next analyzed SREBP1 expression in the liver (Horton et al., 2002; Shimano and Sato, 2017; Yokoyama et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SREBP1 is a key transcription factor for fatty acid biosynthesis.
source: As Acaca, Fasn, and Scd1 are all target genes for sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1, encoded by Srebf1 gene), a key transcription factor for fatty acid biosynthesis, we next analyzed SREBP1 expression in the liver (Horton et al., 2002; Shimano and Sato, 2017; Yokoyama et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There are two isoforms of SREBP1, SREBP1a, and SREBP1c, and the liver predominantly expresses SREBP1c.
source: There are two isoforms of SREBP1, SREBP1a, and SREBP1c, and the liver predominantly expresses SREBP1c (Horton et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The abundance of Srebf1a and Srebf1c mRNA increased in the livers of young Aoah-/- mice.
source: The abundance of Srebf1a and Srebf1c mRNA increased in the livers of young Aoah-/- mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SREBP1 is synthesized as a 125 kDa precursor (full length, flSREBP1) in the endoplasm reticulum, transferred to the Golgi apparatus, and cleaved sequentially by Site-1 protease and Site-2 protease to generate nuclear SREBP1 (nSREBP1, 68 kDa), which enters the nucleus and activates fatty acid biosynthesis gene transcription.
source: SREBP1 is synthesized as a 125 kDa precursor (full length, flSREBP1) in the endoplasm reticulum, transferred to the Golgi apparatus, and cleaved sequentially by Site-1 protease and Site-2 protease to generate nuclear SREBP1 (nSREBP1, 68 kDa), which enters the nucleus and activates fatty acid biosynthesis gene transcription (Horton et al., 2002; Shimano and Sato, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing SREBP1 processing.

claim: The livers mainly had the short-form (68 kDa) nSREBP1 protein, which was significantly more abundant in Aoah-/- mice.
source: The livers mainly had the short-form (68 kDa) nSREBP1 protein, which was significantly more abundant in Aoah-/- mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The short-form SREBP1 was mainly present in nuclei and Aoah-/- mouse liver nuclei contained significantly more SREBP1 than did Aoah+/+ mouse liver nuclei.
source: We separated liver cytosol and nuclei and found that the short-form SREBP1 was mainly present in nuclei and that Aoah-/- mouse liver nuclei contained significantly more SREBP1 than did Aoah+/+ mouse liver nuclei (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The expression of inflammatory genes for serum amyloid A1 (Saa1), Saa2, and Saa3 was significantly higher in Aoah-/- mouse livers.
source: When we analyzed the transcript profiles from co-housed 6–8-week-old Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mouse livers, we noticed that the expression of inflammatory genes for serum amyloid A1 (Saa1), Saa2, and Saa3 was significantly higher in Aoah-/- mouse livers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aoah-/- mouse hepatocytes expressed increased levels of Saa1, Saa2, Saa3, and inflammation regulatory Irak3 mRNA.
source: We isolated hepatocytes from Aoah+/+ and Aoah-/- mice and found that Aoah-/- mouse hepatocytes expressed increased levels of Saa1, Saa2, Saa3, and inflammation regulatory Irak3 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements in isolated hepatocytes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Purified hepatocytes from Aoah-/- mice had increased levels of Acly, Acaca, Acacb, Fasn, and Cd36 mRNA.
source: Purified hepatocytes from Aoah-/- mice had increased levels of Acly, Acaca, Acacb, Fasn, and Cd36 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements in isolated hepatocytes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Purified hepatocytes from Aoah-/- mice had decreased levels of Acot2 and Ppara mRNA.
source: and decreased levels of Acot2 and Ppara mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), changes that may contribute to lipid accumulation as mice grow older.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements in isolated hepatocytes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In young mice, even before hepatic lipid accumulation can be observed, Aoah-/- mouse hepatocytes have altered expression of genes that may promote lipid storage.
source: Thus, in young mice, even before hepatic lipid accumulation can be observed, Aoah-/- mouse hepatocytes have altered expression of genes that may promote lipid storage.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the gene expression data from young mice.

claim: Clodronate-liposome treatment diminished liver Aoah mRNA, confirming that Kupffer cells are the major source of hepatic AOAH.
source: We next used clodronate-liposomes to deplete Kupffer cells and found that clodronate-liposome treatment diminished liver Aoah mRNA, confirming that Kupffer cells are the major source of hepatic AOAH (Shao et al., 2007; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Kupffer cell depletion shown in Figure 5D and citation to previous work.

claim: After clodronate liposome treatment, nSREBP1 levels increased in the liver significantly, resembling Aoah-/- mice.
source: Notably, after clodronate liposome treatment, nSREBP1 levels increased in the liver significantly, resembling Aoah-/- mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data from Kupffer cell depletion experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: AKT-mTOR1-p70 S6-kinase (S6K) activation induces SREBP1c processing in hepatocytes.
source: AKT-mTOR1-p70 S6-kinase (S6K) activation induces SREBP1c processing in hepatocytes (Jeon et al., 2023; Owen et al., 2012; Yecies et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Livers from clodronate-liposome-treated mice had increased AKT and mTOR activation.
source: Livers from clodronate-liposome-treated mice had increased AKT and mTOR activation (Figure 5D), suggesting that when gut-derived LPS cannot be inactivated by AOAH in the liver, bioactive LPS stimulates the mTOR pathway and induces SREBP1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When gut-derived LPS cannot be inactivated by AOAH in the liver, bioactive LPS stimulates the mTOR pathway and induces SREBP1 activation.
source: Livers from clodronate-liposome-treated mice had increased AKT and mTOR activation (Figure 5D), suggesting that when gut-derived LPS cannot be inactivated by AOAH in the liver, bioactive LPS stimulates the mTOR pathway and induces SREBP1 activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that depleting AOAH-expressing Kupffer cells increases mTOR and SREBP1 activation.

claim: Orally gavaged LPS increased hepatic LPS levels in Aoah+/+ mice.
source: We confirmed that orally gavaged (i.g.) LPS increased hepatic LPS levels in Aoah+/+ mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by LPS measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Aoah+/+ mice that received gavaged LPS had increased levels of Srebf1a, Srebf1c, Pcx, Acaca, Acacb, Fasn, Scd1, and Cd36 mRNA in their livers.
source: Like Aoah-/- mice, Aoah+/+ mice that received gavaged LPS had increased levels of Srebf1a, Srebf1c, Pcx, Acaca, Acacb, Fasn, Scd1, and Cd36 mRNA in their livers (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements shown in Figures 6B and C.

claim: LPS administered i.g. increased nSREBP1 in Aoah+/+ mouse livers.
source: LPS administered i.g. also increased nSREBP1 in Aoah+/+ mouse livers (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Elevated AKT-mTOR-S6K activation was found in Aoah-/- mouse livers.
source: Consistently, elevated AKT-mTOR-S6K activation was found in Aoah-/- mouse livers, and when we gave Aoah+/+ mice i.g. LPS, hepatic AKT-mTOR-S6K activity increased (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When Aoah+/+ mice were given i.g. LPS, hepatic AKT-mTOR-S6K activity increased.
source: Consistently, elevated AKT-mTOR-S6K activation was found in Aoah-/- mouse livers, and when we gave Aoah+/+ mice i.g. LPS, hepatic AKT-mTOR-S6K activity increased (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: LPS stimulated mTOR activation and nSREBP1 upregulation in isolated primary hepatocytes.
source: To find out whether LPS can directly stimulate hepatocytes to induce SREBP1 activation, we isolated primary hepatocytes and found that LPS stimulated mTOR activation and nSREBP1 upregulation (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experiments with isolated hepatocytes shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Adding purified Kupffer cells to the hepatocyte culture did not further increase SREBP1 activation.
source: Adding purified Kupffer cells to the hepatocyte culture did not further increase SREBP1 activation, suggesting that LPS directly acts on hepatocytes (Yu et al., 2021), at least in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro co-culture experiments and citation to literature.

claim: LPS directly acts on hepatocytes, at least in vitro.
source: Adding purified Kupffer cells to the hepatocyte culture did not further increase SREBP1 activation, suggesting that LPS directly acts on hepatocytes (Yu et al., 2021), at least in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kupffer cells did not enhance the LPS effect on hepatocytes.

claim: Blocking mTOR activation using torin1 prevented LPS-induced nSREBP1 upregulation.
source: Blocking mTOR activation using torin1 prevented LPS-induced nSREBP1 upregulation (Figure 6E), suggesting that upon LPS stimulation SREBP1 activation depends upon the mTOR pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Upon LPS stimulation SREBP1 activation depends upon the mTOR pathway.
source: Blocking mTOR activation using torin1 prevented LPS-induced nSREBP1 upregulation (Figure 6E), suggesting that upon LPS stimulation SREBP1 activation depends upon the mTOR pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mTOR inhibition blocks LPS-induced SREBP1 activation.

claim: Excessive hepatic LPS derived from the Aoah-/- mouse intestine induces hepatocyte mTOR activity, which increases nSREBP1 abundance.
source: Collectively, these results confirm that excessive hepatic LPS derived from the Aoah-/- mouse intestine induces hepatocyte mTOR activity, which increases nSREBP1 abundance; AOAH prevents hepatic lipid accumulation by inactivating gut-derived LPS.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings in the study.

claim: AOAH prevents hepatic lipid accumulation by inactivating gut-derived LPS.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings in the study.

claim: The intestine and liver are connected by the portal vein, enabling the transport of gut commensal-derived molecules, including Gram-negative bacterial LPS, to the liver.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and established anatomical knowledge.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lipid accumulation in hepatocytes is considered to be the first hit in the pathogenesis of MASLD.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established theory.

claim: Orally gavaged LPS increased hepatic LPS, nSREBP1 abundance, and the expression of nSREBP1's target genes in Aoah+/+ mice.

claim: Gut-derived LPS reaches the liver and promotes fatty acid synthesis.

claim: LPS stimulates hepatocyte directly to promote mTOR activation, which induces lipid accumulation.
